title: Progression of drug resistance or multiple primary lung cancer: a case report and literature review of a patient with mesenchymal–epithelial transition factor exon 14 skipping alterations lung adenocarcinoma
author: Liang Gong; Lihang Zhou; Pan Yang; Fu Xiong; Xin Li; Chunlan Tang
text:
Abstract
Mesenchymal–epithelial transition factor (MET) exon 14 skipping alterations are rare mutations in non-small-cell lung cancer, associated with high malignancy and poor prognosis. This article presents a case of a patient diagnosed with advanced left upper lung adenocarcinoma characterized by a MET14 skipping mutation. Following first-line treatment with crizotinib, there was a significant reduction in the size of the primary lesion; however, during the course of treatment, an increase in size and prominence of solid components were observed in the right upper lung lesion. A biopsy and subsequent genetic testing revealed an epidermal growth factor receptor L858R mutation in the right upper lung adenocarcinoma, indicating the presence of multiple primary lung cancers. The patient opted against surgical intervention and local treatments, choosing instead a combination therapy regimen that included almonertinib and crizotinib. This treatment approach led to a significant reduction in the size of the right upper lung lesion. The patient’s condition has remained stable without any signs of progression, resulting in an overall survival duration exceeding 53 months.
Keywords: almonertinib, crizotinib, MET exon 14 skipping alterations, multiple primary lung cancer
The mesenchymal–epithelial transition factor (MET) gene, also referred to as c-MET, is a proto-oncogene situated on the long arm of human chromosome 7 at the locus 7q21-31. Mutations involving mesenchymal–epithelial transition factor exon 14 skipping alterations (METex14) lead to the loss of the transmembrane domain in the resulting abnormal protein. This alteration impairs the ubiquitination of c-MET protein, thereby increasing its stability and reducing its degradation rate. Consequently, this results in persistent activation of MET signaling pathways and ultimately contributes to tumorigenesis [1]. Individuals with METex14 tend to be older, have a history of smoking, and exhibit a poor response to both chemotherapy and immunotherapy [2,3]. Consequently, the development of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) targeting MET has emerged as a prominent area of research. These inhibitors function by blocking MET activity, which in turn prevents the phosphorylation of downstream kinases. This mechanism effectively halts downstream signal transduction and regulates key processes such as tumor cell proliferation, metastasis, and angiogenesis. Currently, MET inhibitors have received approval for first-line treatment specifically addressing METex14. The evolution of targeted drug resistance is characterized by several mechanisms including gene amplification, second-site mutations, bypass activation, and alterations in pathological types. The patient we reported was newly diagnosed with upper left lung adenocarcinoma, accompanied by double lung and mediastinal metastasis, complicated by a METex14. Following treatment with crizotinib, the lesion in the left upper lung continued to shrink, and the efficacy was evaluated as partial response (PR).
Twenty-five months later, chest computed tomography (CT) revealed that the ground-glass lesion in the right upper lung had significantly enlarged compared with previous imaging, exhibiting increased solid components. A needle biopsy and genetic testing confirmed an epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) L858R mutation in the adenocarcinoma of the left upper lung. Considering factors such as location, imaging findings, and genetic characteristics, progression because of resistance to MET inhibitors was not deemed likely. Ultimately, multiple primary lung cancer (MPLC) was considered. This case analysis is based on both the specific circumstances of this patient and relevant literature.
Case report
A 53-year-old male with a long history of heavy smoking, evidenced by a smoking index of 40 pack-years, presented with the chief complaint that a space occupied in the upper left lung was found during physical examination for 1 month. A chest CT scan conducted at an external hospital on 16 July 2021, revealed a lobulated soft tissue density mass in the upper left lung measuring 68 × 53 mm with unclear boundaries. The mass was closely associated with both the mediastinum and adjacent pleura. Surrounding the mass were several small spots exhibiting increased density and blurred margins. Ground-glass density nodules approximately 8 mm in diameter were identified in the dorsal segment of the right lower lobe, characterized by uniform density and clear borders. In addition, nodules located in the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe measured about 7 mm in diameter and had broad bases attached to the pleura. Multiple enhanced soft tissue nodules were observed within the mediastinum, with a maximum size of 11 × 8 mm noted. The left pleura exhibited thickening and adhesion; ground-glass nodules measuring 8 × 7 mm were also present in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe.
The patient arrived at our hospital on 25 July 2021. Upon admission, contraindications for puncture biopsy were ruled out. A CT-guided puncture biopsy targeting lesions in the left upper lung was performed on 7 August 2021 (Fig. 1). Postoperative pathological analysis confirmed adenocarcinoma of the left upper lung; immunohistochemical results indicated: CK7 (+), TTF-1 (+), CK5/6 (individual +), P40 (−), ALK(D5F3) (−), ALK-N (−), ALK-P (+), Ki-67 (40%+). A real-time quantitative PCR was employed to detect the METex14. Simultaneously, whole-body bone imaging along with brain MRI and abdominal CT scans showed no significant signs indicative of metastasis. Preliminary diagnosis: left upper lung adenocarcinoma (cT4N2M1a stage IVA METex14) with mediastinal lymph node metastatic cancer and intrapulmonary metastatic cancer. The patient declined chemotherapy and initiated oral targeted therapy using crizotinib.
The patient was regularly monitored, and no significant side effects were observed during the course of treatment. On 20 September 2023, a chest CT scan revealed that compared with the previous scan conducted on 12 February 2023, the lesions in the upper lobe of the left lung had slightly decreased in size (27 × 11 mm, ①). Conversely, the lesions in the anterior segment of the upper lobe of the right lung exhibited an increase in size with a maximum diameter measuring approximately 26 × 10 mm, indicating neoplastic activity. No notable changes were detected in other areas (Fig. 2a–e). Evaluation of curative effect: local progression. To elucidate the mechanism underlying drug resistance, a puncture biopsy was performed on the anterior segment of the right upper lobe of the lung following discussions with the patient and their family regarding potential interventions. The biopsy results confirmed adenocarcinoma in the right upper lung. Immunohistochemistry showed CK7 (+), TTF-1 (+), and P63 (individual +), ALK(D5F3) (−), ALK-N (−), ALK-P (+) and Ki-67 (50%). On 3 November 2023, second-generation sequencing of the lung biopsy tissue identified an EGFR exon 21 missense mutation p.L858R. Upon reviewing the patient’s chest imaging and genetic testing results comprehensively, we considered that the enlarged lesions in the anterior segment of the right upper lung may represent MPLC, while unchanged nodules could also indicate multiprimary malignancies. Final diagnosis: (1) Left upper lung adenocarcinoma (cT4N2M0 Stage IIIB with METex14). (1.1) Mediastinal lymph node metastasis. (2) Right upper lung adenocarcinoma (cT3N0M0 Stage IIB with EGFR L858R mutation). (3) MPLCs? (both lungs). For the left upper lung adenocarcinoma, the overall efficacy evaluation is PR, with a progression-free survival (PFS) of 40 months, and no evidence of disease progression to date. In regard to the right upper lung cancer, the patient declined surgery, radiofrequency ablation, and local radiotherapy options. Following discussions with the patient, targeted therapy consisting of ‘crizotinib 250 mg orally twice daily’ combined with ‘almonertinib 110 mg orally once daily’ was initiated on 9 November 2023. During this treatment period, a significant reduction in the lesion associated with right upper lung disease was observed (Fig. 2a1–e1), resulting in an evaluation of PR for this condition as well. The PFS2 is recorded at 13 months. currently, the patient remains alive without disease progression noted thus far, contributing to overall survival (OS) exceeding 53 months.
Discussion
The incidence of METex14 in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) ranges from 0.9 to 4% [4,5]. Most affected individuals are elderly, with a median age of 72.5 years [2], and there is no statistically significant difference observed between the sexes. The prevalence of METex14 varies by histological subtype: approximately 3% in adenocarcinoma [4], 1–2% in squamous cell carcinoma [6,7], and between 13–22% in lung sarcomatoid carcinoma [8,9]. Previous studies have indicated that METex14 does not coexist with other NSCLC driver genes such as EGFR, BRAF, ALK, or ROS1 rearrangements; this suggests that METex14 functions as an independent tumor driver gene [10,11]. Furthermore, these alterations are often associated with high aggressiveness, resistance to antitumor therapies, and poor prognosis [12,13].
For the treatment of METex14 in first-line advanced NSCLC, the 2021 Chinese Society of Clinical Oncology guidelines for diagnosis and treatment recommend the treatment of advanced NSCLC without driver gene mutations; however, the median OS for patients undergoing chemotherapy is only 6.7 months [14]. In addition, the median PFS for patients receiving immunotherapy ranges from 1.9 to 4.9 months [15,16]. Crizotinib, a nonselective multitarget MET inhibitor, has been validated in previous clinical trials as a first-line treatment option for patients with METex14 in advanced NSCLC, demonstrating a median PFS of 7.3–8.5 months – significantly longer than that achieved with chemotherapy [17–19]. In light of the clinical studies available at the time, one patient elected to forego chemotherapy and instead receive crizotinib-targeted therapy for a period exceeding 2 years. During this interval, the primary lesion exhibited a reduction in size without evidence of disease progression, as evaluated according to PR criteria. As research progresses, highly selective single-target MET inhibitors, including capmatinib, tepotinib, savolitinib, glumetinib, and vebreltinib, are now recommended as first-line treatments that specifically target METex14 [20–24].
It is noteworthy that, during targeted treatment with MET inhibitors, the ground-glass nodules in the upper right lung tissue exhibited an increase in size and a greater solid component than observed before treatment. Given the potential for drug resistance to develop, a lung puncture biopsy and genetic testing were conducted, which revealed that while the tissue type remained consistent, there were significant genomic differences; however, the enlargement of the lesion in the right upper lung may be attributed to MPLC or intrapulmonary metastasis.
MPLC denotes the coexistence of two or more primary lung cancers in a single patient’s lungs, occurring either concurrently or in a sequential manner. This condition is classified into two categories: synchronous MPLC (sMPLC) and metachronous MPLC (mMPLC) [25]. Despite the absence of a universally accepted standard, three commonly utilized diagnostic criteria for sMPLC and mMPLC are prevalent in clinical practice [26–28].
The latest data suggest that primary drug resistance to MET inhibitors is associated with mutations in the MET gene, including H1094, G1163, L1195, D1228, Y1230, and allele amplification of MET 14 exon [29]. Secondary drug resistance to MET-TKIs encompasses a range of genetic alterations, including mutations in TP53, KRAS, HER3, and BRAF genes, as well as EGFR amplification, RAS-MAPK, and RTK-RAS-PI3K bypass activation; however, no EGFR-sensitive mutation is present [29,30]. In conclusion, the tuberosity in the anterior right upper lobe of the lung of the patient before crizotinib treatment exhibited a ground-glass appearance, which manifested concurrently with the larger lesions in the left upper lobe. Its molecular biological characteristics were distinct from those of the larger lesions in the left upper lobe (EGFR 18 L858R mutation and METex14, respectively). Accordingly, the patient in our report was deemed to be a suitable candidate for sMPLC. The other nodules in the lung, which were initially considered to be metastatic cancer, did not undergo shrinkage or disappearance in conjunction with the shrinkage of the larger lesions in the left upper lung treated with crizotinib. Furthermore, there is a high probability that these lesions represent multiple primary cancers. It is imperative that rigorous follow-up is conducted in the subsequent stages, and that lung puncture biopsy is performed when necessary (such as in cases of enlargement) to further identify the pathological types or molecular biological characteristics.
For patients diagnosed with early-stage MPLC, surgical intervention [27], radiotherapy, and local radiofrequency ablation represent viable treatment options [31,32]. The prevalence of EGFR mutations in MPLC among Asian patients ranges from 45.8 to 76.0%, indicating that targeted therapy may represent a more effective treatment strategy for this patient population [33]. Nevertheless, the efficacy of immunotherapy remains uncertain [34]. The patient elected to pursue a targeted therapeutic approach, comprising the combination of crizotinib and almonertinib. The lesion in the right upper lobe of the lung exhibited a notable reduction in size, whereas the lesion in the left upper lobe demonstrated no appreciable change compared with the previous assessment. The assessed disease demonstrated a PFS2 of 13 months, with the patient remaining alive without any signs of disease progression. This resulted in an overall OS exceeding 53 months.
In conclusion, MET-TKIs represent the optimal first-line treatment option for advanced METex14. In addition to the initial diagnosis of lung cancer, it is of paramount importance to differentiate between MPLC and intrapulmonary metastasis. This distinction is of particular importance when assessing disease progression because of drug resistance or metastasis, as the size of nodules increases during treatment, thereby influencing subsequent therapeutic decisions. The combination of genome-wide next-generation sequencing with histopathology and imaging techniques represents a promising approach for differentiating MPLC cases. Surgical intervention remains the primary treatment modality for MPLC; however, alternative options, such as stereotactic ablative radiotherapy and local ablation, may be employed for patients who are not suitable candidates for surgical intervention. It is possible that targeted therapies, potentially combined with surgical approaches, may emerge as viable options for patients who have positive driver genes. Nevertheless, challenges remain with regard to the application of immunotherapy. Although a range of treatment strategies for MPLC are currently available, further research is necessary to develop more personalized therapeutic options that are tailored to the specific needs of individual patients.
